questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to DILIGENT.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Diligent means showing steady, careful effort, i.e. hard-working. Intelligent is a different quality, and careless is the opposite.

questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to CANDID.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Candid means honest and direct, i.e. frank. Secretive and cunning are nearly opposite, and polite is unrelated.

questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to ABUNDANT.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Abundant means existing in large quantities, i.e. plentiful. Scarce is its antonym.

questions.question_text: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to TRANSPARENT.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Transparent means that light passes through; opaque means that it does not. Clear is a synonym.

questions.question_text: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to EXPAND.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: To expand is to become larger; to contract is to become smaller. Enlarge and extend are synonyms.

questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: The committee has not yet \_\_\_\_\_\_ a decision on the proposal.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Reach a decision' is the standard collocation. 'Arrived' would need 'at'; 'done a decision' and 'made up a decision' are not idiomatic.

questions.question_text: Fill in the blanks: She is good \_\_\_\_\_\_ mathematics but weak \_\_\_\_\_\_ spelling.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The idioms are 'good at' a subject and 'weak in' a subject. Only the first pair puts 'at' after 'good'.

questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: Neither the manager nor his assistants \_\_\_\_\_\_ present at the meeting.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, here the plural 'assistants', and the past tense fits 'at the meeting'. So 'were'.

questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) Each of the students / (B) have submitted / (C) the project / (D) before the deadline.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Each' is singular, so the verb must be 'has submitted'. The error is in part B.

questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) He has been living / (B) in Pune / (C) since five years / (D) and likes it there.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Since' is used with a point in time (since 2020); a period of time takes 'for'. It should be 'for five years'. The error is in part C.

questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) If I would have known / (B) about the traffic, / (C) I would have left / (D) home earlier.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In a third conditional, the if-clause takes the past perfect: 'If I had known…'. 'Would have' belongs only in the main clause (part C, which is correct). The error is in part A.

questions.question_text:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: to the station
Q: I ran all the way
R: but still missed
S: the last bus home
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'I ran all the way (Q) to the station (P) but still missed (R) the last bus home (S).' QRSP gives 'the last bus home to the station', which contradicts itself (home or the station?). PRQS breaks 'missed … the last bus' apart, and RSQP begins with 'but' and leaves 'to the station' hanging.

questions.question_text:
The sentence begins: 'The children…'. Rearrange the parts to complete it:
P: that they fell asleep
Q: were so tired
R: on the sofa
S: before dinner was served
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'The children were so tired (Q) that they fell asleep (P) on the sofa (R) before dinner was served (S).' The 'so … that' pattern needs Q before P. Each other option puts 'that they fell asleep' before 'were so tired', which is ungrammatical.

questions.question_text:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: the book
Q: that you lent me
R: is
S: very interesting
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'The book (P) that you lent me (Q) is (R) very interesting (S).' The relative clause Q must come right after the noun it describes, 'the book', and then the verb 'is' and its complement follow. PRQS, QRPS and RQSP all separate the clause from its noun or misplace the verb, giving ungrammatical strings.

questions.question_text:
Match each word in List I with its meaning in List II.
List I: (a) Benevolent (b) Meticulous (c) Ephemeral (d) Gregarious
List II: (i) lasting a very short time (ii) fond of the company of others (iii) kind and generous (iv) very careful about detail
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Benevolent = kind and generous (iii); meticulous = very careful about detail (iv); ephemeral = lasting a very short time (i); gregarious = fond of company (ii).

Passage: In the dry parts of western India, people once solved the problem of water not by building walls around it but by digging down to meet it. The result was the stepwell, known as a vav or baoli: a well so wide that a flight of steps could lead from the ground to the water below. As the water level rose and fell with the seasons, villagers simply walked down or up to reach it.
Stepwells were more than water tanks. The cool, shaded air at the bottom made them places to rest in the heat of the day, and travellers on long trade routes often stopped at them. Many were decorated with carved pillars, balconies and sculpted figures, because the people who paid for them saw the gift of water as an act of merit. Some, like Rani ki Vav in Gujarat, are now World Heritage sites.
Their decline began when piped water and hand pumps arrived. Once water could be drawn without walking down a hundred steps, many stepwells were abandoned, filled with rubbish or used as dumps. Yet some are being given new life. Volunteers have cleared silt, repaired walls and let rainwater flow back in. The lesson, they say, is practical as well as historical: structures that store rain where it falls may be useful again in regions where groundwater is running low.

The passage is mainly about:

options.B: stepwells: their purpose, beauty, decline and revival
options.C: the history of trade routes in western India
options.D: how piped water systems are built in cities

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage explains what stepwells were, why they were decorated, why they were abandoned and how some are being restored.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Most students know the feeling of studying late into the night and then struggling to remember anything the next day. Research on sleep suggests that this is not just bad luck. During sleep, the brain appears to replay and strengthen what was learned during the day, helping to move new information into long-term memory. A student who sleeps well after studying may therefore recall more than one who stays awake revising for the same extra hours.
Sleep matters for another reason: attention. A tired mind finds it harder to focus, makes more careless mistakes and is slower to solve problems. These effects are small after one bad night but add up when short sleep becomes a habit.
Teenagers face a particular difficulty. During adolescence the body's internal clock tends to shift later, so many teenagers do not feel sleepy until late at night, yet school often begins early in the morning. Some schools that moved their start times later have reported better attendance and alertness, though researchers caution that results vary and that more studies are needed.
None of this means that studying late is always a mistake; an occasional late night before an exam may be unavoidable. But the evidence suggests that sleep is part of studying, not a break from it. A regular bedtime, a dark room and keeping phones away from the bed are simple steps that cost nothing and may help.

According to the passage, during sleep the brain appears to:

options.A: work faster than during the day
options.D: replay and strengthen what was learned during the day

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The first paragraph says the brain 'appears to replay and strengthen what was learned', helping to move it into long-term memory.

Passage: Arjun's family had moved cities in the middle of the school year, and on his first morning he walked into Class IX with his bag held tightly in front of him, as if it were a shield. The teacher pointed to the only empty seat, on the last bench by the window. He sat down and looked at the board without really reading it.
At the break, the others drifted out in noisy groups. Arjun stayed, pretending to search his bag. He knew nobody here, and he had decided, quite firmly, that it was easier not to try.
"You can have the window seat," said a voice. A boy with a patched blue bag had stopped beside the bench. "I always sit here, but nobody comes this far back anyway." He laughed, as though it were a joke against himself. "I'm Imran. We have maths next. Mr Rao gives homework before he even says good morning."
Arjun almost smiled. "Is it hard?"
"Only if you're alone," said Imran, and pulled out a spare notebook. "Copy the last class's notes from mine. I'll show you which ones matter."
By the end of the day Arjun had stopped holding his bag like a shield. He did not know yet whether he would like the city or the school. But the last bench, he thought, was not quite as far from everything as it had looked that morning.

Why did Arjun hold his bag in front of him 'as if it were a shield'?

options.B: He was angry with his teacher
options.C: He felt nervous and defensive in a new place

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A shield protects. The image shows that Arjun felt unsafe and guarded on his first day in a new school.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Arjun's family had moved cities in the middle of the school year, and on his first morning he walked into Class IX with his bag held tightly in front of him, as if it were a shield. The teacher pointed to the only empty seat, on the last bench by the window. He sat down and looked at the board without really reading it.
At the break, the others drifted out in noisy groups. Arjun stayed, pretending to search his bag. He knew nobody here, and he had decided, quite firmly, that it was easier not to try.
"You can have the window seat," said a voice. A boy with a patched blue bag had stopped beside the bench. "I always sit here, but nobody comes this far back anyway." He laughed, as though it were a joke against himself. "I'm Imran. We have maths next. Mr Rao gives homework before he even says good morning."
Arjun almost smiled. "Is it hard?"
"Only if you're alone," said Imran, and pulled out a spare notebook. "Copy the last class's notes from mine. I'll show you which ones matter."
By the end of the day Arjun had stopped holding his bag like a shield. He did not know yet whether he would like the city or the school. But the last bench, he thought, was not quite as far from everything as it had looked that morning.

Why did Arjun stay in the classroom at the break?

options.A: He had a test to prepare for
options.C: The teacher asked him to stay
options.D: He had decided it was easier not to try to make friends

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says he 'had decided, quite firmly, that it was easier not to try'.

questions.question_text:
Passage: Few people write by hand for long these days. Messages are typed, notes are dictated and even shopping lists live on phones. It is easy to say that handwriting is a skill whose time has passed, like lighting a lamp with a match. But before we let it go, we might ask what it quietly does for us.
Several small studies suggest that students who take notes by hand tend to understand lecture material a little better than those who type. The explanation offered is simple: handwriting is slow, so the writer cannot copy everything and must decide what matters. Typing is fast enough to record almost every word, and the typist may leave the lecture with pages of text and little thought behind them.
Handwriting also carries something of the writer. A letter in a familiar hand can comfort a reader in a way that a printed page cannot, and a signature is still trusted as proof of a person's presence.
None of this is an argument against keyboards, which are faster, tidier and indispensable for long documents. It is only an argument against giving up one tool simply because another has arrived. The sensible course is to keep both, using the pen when we want to think and the keyboard when we want to produce.

The main idea of the passage is that:

options.B: handwriting still has value and should be kept alongside typing

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author gives reasons for keeping handwriting and ends by recommending that we keep both tools.

questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to PRUDENT.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Prudent means acting with care and good judgement, i.e. cautious. Reckless is its antonym.

questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to CONCEAL.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: To conceal is to keep something from being seen or known, i.e. to hide. Reveal is its antonym.

questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to SCARCE.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Scarce means in short supply, i.e. rare or hard to find. Plentiful is its antonym.

questions.question_text: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to GENEROUS.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Generous means willing to give freely; miserly means unwilling to spend or give. Kind is close to the original meaning, not opposite.

questions.question_text: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to VICTORY.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Victory is winning; defeat is losing. Triumph and success are synonyms of victory.

questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: She is allergic \_\_\_\_\_\_ peanuts.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The correct preposition after 'allergic' is 'to'.

questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: I have lived in this town \_\_\_\_\_\_ 2015.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Since' is used with a point in time (2015). 'For' would be used with a period, such as 'for nine years'.

questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: Each of the players \_\_\_\_\_\_ a medal at the ceremony.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Each' takes a singular verb, so 'have received', 'were receiving' and 'are given' (all plural) are wrong. 'Received' works as a past-tense verb with a singular subject.

questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: Neither of the two answers \_\_\_\_\_\_ correct.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Neither' is treated as singular, so the singular verb 'is' is required.

questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) The news about the floods / (B) were broadcast / (C) on every channel / (D) last night.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'News' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb. It should be 'was broadcast'. The error is in part B.

questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) She said me / (B) that she would / (C) come to the party / (D) tomorrow.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Said' cannot take a direct person object. It should be 'told me' (or 'said to me'). The error is in part A.

questions.question_text:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: the scientists
Q: a new species
R: discovered
S: in the deep sea
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'The scientists (P) discovered (R) a new species (Q) in the deep sea (S).' The subject comes first, then the verb, then its object, then the place.

questions.question_text: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: a person who can speak many languages.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A polyglot knows and can use several languages. A pedant is overly concerned with detail, a philanthropist helps others with money, and a pessimist expects the worst.

questions.question_text: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: a large cage or building in which birds are kept.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: An aviary is a place for keeping birds. An apiary is for bees, an aquarium is for fish and an armoury is for weapons.

If A = [2, 1; 3, 4] and B = [1, 0; −1, 2], then AB equals:

*(Matrices are written row by row; rows are separated by ";".)*
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Row × column: (1,1) = 2·1 + 1·(−1) = 1; (1,2) = 2·0 + 1·2 = 2; (2,1) = 3·1 + 4·(−1) = −1; (2,2) = 3·0 + 4·2 = 8. (Option A is BA, which is different because matrix multiplication is not commutative. Option D multiplies entry by entry, and Option C adds the matrices.)

questions.question_text: If A is a 3 × 3 skew-symmetric matrix, the sum of its diagonal entries is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In a skew-symmetric matrix Aᵀ = −A, so every diagonal entry satisfies aᵢᵢ = −aᵢᵢ, i.e. aᵢᵢ = 0. The sum is 0 whatever the other entries are.

questions.question_text:
The inverse of A = [2, 3; 1, 2] is:

*(Matrices are written row by row; rows are separated by ";".)*
questions.pedagogical_explanation: ∣A∣ = 2·2 − 3·1 = 1. For a 2 × 2 matrix, A⁻¹ = (1/∣A∣) × (swap the diagonal entries and change the sign of the other two), which gives Option B. Check: A·A⁻¹ = I.

questions.question_text:
The value of the determinant ∣1, 2, 3; 0, 4, 5; 1, 0, 6∣ is:

*(Matrices are written row by row; rows are separated by ";".)*
Using determinants, what is the area of the triangle with vertices (1, 0), (6, 0) and (4, 3)?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Area = ½ ∣det∣ of the rows (x, y, 1): ½ ∣1(0 − 3) − 0 + 1(18 − 0)∣ = ½ × 15 = 7.5. (Check: base 5 on the x-axis, height 3 gives ½ × 5 × 3 = 7.5.)

questions.question_text: If y = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1, what is the value of d²y/dx² at x = 1?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: dy/dx = 3x² − 12x + 9 and d²y/dx² = 6x − 12. At x = 1 this is −6. (0 is the value of dy/dx at x = 1.)

questions.question_text: The function f(x) = x³ − 3x is strictly decreasing on the interval:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 3(x − 1)(x + 1), which is negative exactly when −1 < x < 1. On (1, ∞) and (−∞, −1), f is increasing.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum value of f(x) = −x² + 4x + 5?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: f′(x) = −2x + 4 = 0 gives x = 2, and f″(x) = −2 < 0, so x = 2 is a maximum. f(2) = −4 + 8 + 5 = 9.

questions.question_text: Evaluate ∫₀¹ x eˣ dx.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: By parts with u = x, dv = eˣ dx: ∫ x eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ. From 0 to 1: (e − e) − (0 − 1) = 1.

questions.question_text: ∫ dx / (x² + 9) equals:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Use the standard result ∫ dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + C with a = 3.

questions.question_text: Evaluate ∫₀^{π/2} sin²x dx.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2. Integrating from 0 to π/2 gives [x/2 − sin 2x/4] = π/4 − 0 = π/4.

questions.question_text: What is the area of the region bounded by the curve y = x², the x-axis and the lines x = 0 and x = 3?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Area = ∫₀³ x² dx = [x³/3] from 0 to 3 = 27/3 = 9.

questions.question_text: What are the order and the degree of the differential equation (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)⁴ + y = 0?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The order is that of the highest derivative present, d²y/dx², so it is 2. The degree is the power of that highest-order derivative (the equation is a polynomial in the derivatives), which is 3.

questions.question_text: If dy/dx = y/x and y = 2 when x = 1, what is y when x = 3?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Separate variables: dy/y = dx/x, so log∣y∣ = log∣x∣ + c and y = kx. y(1) = 2 gives k = 2, so y = 2x and y(3) = 6.

questions.question_text: Two fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers is 8?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Out of 36 equally likely outcomes, a sum of 8 comes from (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3) and (6,2): 5 outcomes. P = 5/36.

questions.question_text: Maximise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x ≤ 3, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. The maximum value of Z is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The corner points of the feasible region are (0, 0), (3, 0), (3, 1) and (0, 4). Z = 0, 9, 11 and 8 there, so the maximum is 11, at (3, 1). (12 would need x = 4, which breaks x ≤ 3.)

options.C: reflexive and symmetric, but not transitive

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Reflexive: (1,1), (2,2) and (3,3) are all present. Symmetric: (1,2) and (2,1) are both present. Transitive: every chain is closed, e.g. (1,2) and (2,1) give (1,1), which is in R. So R is an equivalence relation, with classes {1, 2} and {3}.

questions.question_text: How many one-one functions are there from A = {1, 2, 3} to B = {a, b, c, d}?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 1 can go to any of 4 elements, 2 to any of the remaining 3, and 3 to any of the remaining 2: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. (64 = 4³ counts all functions.)

questions.question_text: What is the principal value of sin⁻¹(−1/2)?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The principal range of sin⁻¹ is [−π/2, π/2]. sin(−π/6) = −1/2, and −π/6 lies in that range. (sin 7π/6 is also −1/2, but 7π/6 is outside the principal range.)

questions.question_text: f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2, and f(2) = k. For which value of k is f continuous at x = 2?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: For x ≠ 2, f(x) = (x − 2)(x + 2)/(x − 2) = x + 2, which tends to 4 as x → 2. Continuity needs f(2) = 4, so k = 4.

questions.question_text: If y = e²ˣ sin x, then dy/dx at x = 0 is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Product rule: dy/dx = 2e²ˣ sin x + e²ˣ cos x. At x = 0: 0 + 1·1 = 1.

questions.question_text: The radius of a circle is increasing at 2 cm/s. How fast is its area increasing when the radius is 5 cm?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A = πr², so dA/dt = 2πr · dr/dt = 2π × 5 × 2 = 20π cm²/s.

questions.question_text: What is the area of the parallelogram whose adjacent sides are a = î + 2ĵ and b = 3î + k̂?
What is the angle between two lines whose direction ratios are 1, 1, 0 and 0, 1, 1?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: cos θ = ∣a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂∣ / (√(a₁² + b₁² + c₁²) √(a₂² + b₂² + c₂²)) = (0 + 1 + 0)/(√2 · √2) = 1/2, so θ = 60°.

questions.question_text: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Which statement is true?

options.A: P(A ∣ B) = 0.5, and A and B are independent
options.B: P(A ∣ B) = 0.5, and A and B are not independent
options.C: P(A ∣ B) = 0.2, and A and B are mutually exclusive
options.D: P(A ∣ B) = 0.4, and A and B are independent

questions.pedagogical_explanation: P(A ∣ B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5, which equals P(A). Also P(A)P(B) = 0.2 = P(A ∩ B), so A and B are independent. They are not mutually exclusive, since P(A ∩ B) ≠ 0.

*(Matrices are written row by row; rows are separated by ";".)*
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A² = A × A. Row × column: (1,1) = 1·1 + 2·3 = 7; (1,2) = 1·2 + 2·4 = 10; (2,1) = 3·1 + 4·3 = 15; (2,2) = 3·2 + 4·4 = 22. Squaring each entry (Option D) is not matrix multiplication.

questions.question_text: If A is a 2 × 2 matrix with ∣A∣ = 5, then ∣3A∣ equals:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: For an n × n matrix, ∣kA∣ = kⁿ∣A∣. Here n = 2 and k = 3, so ∣3A∣ = 3² × 5 = 45. (15 forgets that both rows are multiplied by 3.)

questions.question_text:
If [x + y, 2; 5, x − y] = [7, 2; 5, 1], then the value of xy is:

*(Matrices are written row by row; rows are separated by ";".)*
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Equal matrices have equal entries: x + y = 7 and x − y = 1. Adding gives x = 4, and then y = 3. So xy = 12.

questions.question_text:
The value of the determinant ∣1, 1, 1; 1, 2, 3; 1, 4, 9∣ is:

*(Matrices are written row by row; rows are separated by ";".)*
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Subtract the first row from the second and third: rows become (0, 1, 2) and (0, 3, 8). Expanding along the first column gives 1 × (1·8 − 2·3) = 2.

questions.question_text: If A is a 3 × 3 matrix with ∣A∣ = 4, then ∣adj A∣ equals:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: For an n × n matrix, ∣adj A∣ = ∣A∣ⁿ⁻¹. With n = 3 this is 4² = 16.

questions.question_text: If y = xˣ (x > 0), then dy/dx at x = 1 is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take logs: log y = x log x, so y′/y = log x + 1 and y′ = xˣ(1 + log x). At x = 1: 1 × (1 + 0) = 1.

questions.question_text: f(x) = kx + 1 for x ≤ 5 and f(x) = 3x − 5 for x > 5. For which value of k is f continuous at x = 5?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The left value is 5k + 1 and the right limit is 3(5) − 5 = 10. Continuity needs 5k + 1 = 10, so k = 9/5.

questions.question_text: What is the equation of the tangent to the curve y = x² at the point (1, 1)?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: dy/dx = 2x = 2 at x = 1. The tangent through (1, 1) is y − 1 = 2(x − 1), i.e. y = 2x − 1.

questions.question_text: A rectangle has a perimeter of 40 cm. What is the largest area it can have?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: With sides w and 20 − w the area is w(20 − w). Its derivative 20 − 2w is zero at w = 10, giving a square of side 10 and area 100 cm², which is a maximum because the second derivative is negative.

questions.question_text: ∫ x/(x² + 1) dx equals:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Put u = x² + 1, so du = 2x dx and x dx = du/2. The integral becomes (1/2) ∫ du/u = (1/2) log∣u∣ + C.

questions.question_text: Evaluate ∫₀¹ x² e^{x³} dx.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Put u = x³, du = 3x² dx. The limits stay 0 to 1, and the integral is (1/3) ∫₀¹ eᵘ du = (e − 1)/3.

questions.question_text: ∫ dx/√(4 − x²) equals:

questions.question_text: What is the area enclosed between the curves y = x and y = x² ?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The curves meet at x = 0 and x = 1, and y = x lies above y = x² in between. Area = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6.

questions.question_text: The integrating factor of the differential equation dy/dx + (2/x) y = x² (x > 0) is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The integrating factor is e^{∫P dx} with P = 2/x. ∫(2/x) dx = 2 log x, so the factor is e^{2 log x} = x².

questions.question_text: If dy/dx = y and y = 1 when x = 0, then the value of y at x = 1 is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Separating variables, dy/y = dx gives log y = x + c. y(0) = 1 gives c = 0, so y = eˣ and y(1) = e.

questions.question_text: A fair coin is tossed four times. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: P(no head) = (1/2)⁴ = 1/16. So P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/16 = 15/16.

questions.question_text: How many reflexive relations can be defined on a set with 3 elements?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A relation on a 3-element set is a subset of the 9 ordered pairs. For reflexivity the 3 pairs (a, a) must be included, and the other 6 pairs are free: 2⁶ = 64. (512 = 2⁹ counts all relations.)

questions.question_text: The function f: R → R defined by f(x) = x² is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: f(2) = f(−2) = 4, so f is not one-one. Its values are never negative, so the range is [0, ∞) and not all of R: f is not onto.

questions.question_text: If f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², then (g∘f)(2) equals:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: (g∘f)(2) = g(f(2)) = g(5) = 25. (9 is (f∘g)(2) = f(4), the composition in the other order.)

questions.question_text: The value of tan⁻¹ 1 + tan⁻¹ 2 + tan⁻¹ 3 is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: tan⁻¹ 1 = π/4. For tan⁻¹ 2 + tan⁻¹ 3, ab = 6 > 1, so the sum is π + tan⁻¹((2 + 3)/(1 − 6)) = π + tan⁻¹(−1) = π − π/4 = 3π/4. Total = π/4 + 3π/4 = π.

questions.question_text: The value of sin(cos⁻¹(3/5)) is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let θ = cos⁻¹(3/5), so cos θ = 3/5 with θ in [0, π]. Then sin θ = √(1 − 9/25) = 4/5, which is positive in that range.

questions.question_text: What is the principal value of cos⁻¹(−1/2)?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The principal range of cos⁻¹ is [0, π]. cos(2π/3) = −1/2 and 2π/3 lies in that range. (4π/3 also has cosine −1/2 but is outside the range.)

questions.question_text: If x = at² and y = 2at, then dy/dx at t = 1 is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: dx/dt = 2at and dy/dt = 2a, so dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 2a/(2at) = 1/t. At t = 1 this is 1.

questions.question_text: Rolle's theorem is applied to f(x) = x² − 4x + 3 on [1, 3]. The value of c is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: f(1) = f(3) = 0, so Rolle's theorem applies. f′(x) = 2x − 4 = 0 gives c = 2, which lies in (1, 3).

questions.question_text: The local maximum value of f(x) = x³ − 12x is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: f′(x) = 3x² − 12 = 0 gives x = ±2. f″(x) = 6x is negative at x = −2, so that is the local maximum: f(−2) = −8 + 24 = 16. (−16 is the local minimum at x = 2.)

questions.question_text: The edge of a cube increases at 3 cm/s. How fast is its volume increasing when the edge is 2 cm?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: V = a³, so dV/dt = 3a² · da/dt = 3 × 4 × 3 = 36 cm³/s.

questions.question_text: If ∣a∣ = 3, ∣b∣ = 4 and a · b = 6, then the angle between a and b is:
The vectors a = î + 2ĵ + 3k̂ and b = 3î − ĵ + λk̂ are perpendicular. The value of λ is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Perpendicular vectors have a · b = 0: 3 − 2 + 3λ = 0, so λ = −1/3.

questions.question_text: What is the distance of the point (1, 2, 3) from the plane x + 2y + 2z = 3?
A line has direction ratios 2, 3, 6. The cosine of the angle it makes with the x-axis is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The length of (2, 3, 6) is √(4 + 9 + 36) = 7, so the direction cosines are 2/7, 3/7 and 6/7. The cosine with the x-axis is the first one, 2/7.

questions.question_text: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.65. Then:

options.B: A and B are mutually exclusive

questions.pedagogical_explanation: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B) = 0.8 − 0.65 = 0.15. This equals P(A)P(B) = 0.15, so the events are independent. They are not mutually exclusive because P(A ∩ B) ≠ 0.

questions.question_text: A random variable X follows a binomial distribution with n = 6 and p = 1/3. Its mean and variance are:
Minimise Z = 2x + 3y subject to x + y ≥ 4, x ≥ 1, y ≥ 0. The minimum value of Z is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The corner points of this (unbounded) region are (1, 3) and (4, 0). Z = 11 at (1, 3) and Z = 8 at (4, 0). Because Z has positive coefficients, it only grows along the open directions, so the minimum is 8.
